name: Martin Luther
info: Martin Luther (1483–1546) was a German priest, theologian and former Augustinian friar whose Ninety-five Theses of 1517 made him the seminal figure of the Protestant Reformation and whose theological beliefs form the basis of Lutheranism.

facts.born: 10 November 1483 in Eisleben, County of Mansfeld, in the Holy Roman Empire; eldest son of Hans Luder (later Luther), a leaseholder of copper mines and smelters, and Margarethe, née Lindemann
facts.died: 18 February 1546 in Eisleben, aged 62, after chest pains and an apoplectic stroke; buried in the Schlosskirche in Wittenberg
facts.role: Augustinian friar (from 1505); priest (ordained 1507); Doctor of Theology and chair of theology at the University of Wittenberg (from 1512); provincial vicar of Saxony and Thuringia (1515); excommunicated and declared an outlaw in 1521
facts.known: the Ninety-five Theses (1517); the doctrine of justification by faith alone; his refusal to recant at the Diet of Worms (1521); his German translation of the Bible (1522–1534); the Large and Small Catechisms (1529) and his hymns; his marriage to Katharina von Bora; his writings against the Jews (1543)

t: An Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, Luther protested against the sale of indulgences in 1517 and by 1521 had been excommunicated by Pope Leo X and declared an outlaw by Emperor Charles V.

He taught that justification is received only as a gift of God's grace through faith and that the Bible is the only source of divinely revealed knowledge, and he gave German speakers a Bible, a Mass, catechisms and hymns in their own language.
He called on the nobles to put down the peasant rebels of 1525 and in 1543 advocated burning synagogues and expelling the Jews, writings that were quoted in Nazi Germany.
dyk: Luther is often quoted as saying "Here I stand. I can do no other" at the Diet of Worms, but recent scholars consider the evidence for these words unreliable: they appear only in later versions of the speech, not in witness accounts.
ev: Born in Eisleben, in the County of Mansfeld, to Hans Luder and his wife Margarethe
Receives his master's degree at Erfurt, abandons law and enters St Augustine's Monastery there
Writes to Archbishop Albert of Mainz against the sale of indulgences, enclosing the Ninety-five Theses
Excommunicated by Pope Leo X; refuses to recant before the Diet of Worms and is declared an outlaw by the Edict of Worms
Writes against the rebels of the Peasants' War and marries Katharina von Bora, a former nun
The whole Bible in his German translation is published, twelve years after his New Testament
Publishes On the Jews and Their Lies, advocating the burning of synagogues and the expulsion of the Jews
Dies in Eisleben after an apoplectic stroke and is buried in the Schlosskirche in Wittenberg

sections.early:
Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 in Eisleben, in the County of Mansfeld in the Holy Roman Empire, to Hans Luder (later Luther) and his wife Margarethe, née Lindemann. In 1484 the family moved to Mansfeld, where his father was a leaseholder of copper mines and smelters and, from 1492, a town councillor. The Lutheran scholar Martin E. Marty describes his mother as a hard-working woman of "trading-class stock and middling means"; Luther's enemies labelled her a whore and bath attendant.

Hans was determined that Martin, his eldest son, should become a lawyer. He sent him to Latin schools in Mansfeld, in Magdeburg in 1497 and in Eisenach in 1498. In 1501, at age 17, he entered the University of Erfurt, and he received his master's degree in 1505. He enrolled in law as his father wished but dropped out almost immediately. Drawn to theology and philosophy, he was influenced by two tutors, Bartholomaeus Arnoldi von Usingen and Jodocus Trutfetter, who taught him to test everything by experience; but he came to hold that reason could not lead men to God, who could be known only through divine revelation.

Two stories are told of his sudden decision to become a monk. Philip Melanchthon's is that he was shocked by the sudden death of a university friend. The other is that on 2 July 1505 a lightning bolt struck near him as he rode back to university, and he cried out, "Help! Saint Anna, I will become a monk!" He entered St Augustine's Monastery in Erfurt on 17 July 1505. His father was furious at what he saw as a waste of his education.
sections.rise:
As an Augustinian friar Luther devoted himself to fasting, long hours in prayer, pilgrimage and frequent confession, and he described the period as one of deep spiritual despair. His superior, Johann von Staupitz, ordered him to pursue an academic career. He was ordained in Erfurt Cathedral on 3 April 1507 and in 1508 began teaching theology at the University of Wittenberg. He was awarded his Doctor of Theology on 19 October 1512 and two days later succeeded Staupitz as chair of theology, the position he held for the rest of his career. In 1515 he was made provincial vicar of Saxony and Thuringia.

Lecturing on the Psalms, Hebrews, Romans and Galatians, he became convinced that the Church had lost sight of central truths of Christianity, above all justification by faith alone through God's grace. On 31 October 1517 he wrote to Albert of Brandenburg, Archbishop of Mainz, protesting against the sale of indulgences and enclosed his "Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences", the Ninety-five Theses. According to one account he nailed them to the door of All Saints' Church in Wittenberg that day; the story rests on a statement by Melanchthon, who was not yet in Wittenberg, and the Catholic historian Erwin Iserloh argued in the 1960s that no posting took place. Hans Hillerbrand writes that Luther intended a scholarly objection, not a confrontation with the Church.

The Theses were printed in several places in Germany in 1517 and translated into German in January 1518, and his writings reached France, England and Italy as early as 1519.
sections.deeds:
At the Leipzig disputation of 1519 Luther asserted that neither popes nor church councils were infallible. In 1520 he published To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church and On the Freedom of a Christian, and on 10 December he publicly burned the bull Exsurge Domine, which required him to recant 41 sentences. Pope Leo X excommunicated him on 3 January 1521. Before the Diet of Worms in April he refused to recant: "my conscience is captive to the Word of God". The Edict of Worms of 25 May 1521 declared him an outlaw.

Frederick III, Elector of Saxony, had him taken in a staged rescue to the Wartburg Castle, where he translated the New Testament from Greek into German; it was published in 1522, and the whole Bible followed in 1534. Written in the German of the Saxon chancellery, intelligible to northern and southern Germans alike, it fostered a standard version of the language. Returning to Wittenberg on 6 March 1522, he preached the eight Invocavit Sermons, urging trust in God's word rather than violence to bring about change.

From 1525 to 1529 he organised a new church in the Electorate of Saxony with Elector John the Steadfast: a supervisory body, a German Mass published in 1526 with congregational singing and communion in both bread and wine, and in 1529 the Large and Small Catechisms. He wrote hymns such as "Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott". On 13 June 1525 he married Katharina von Bora, a former nun, which set the seal of approval on clerical marriage; she bore six children.
sections.opponents:
Rome answered Luther with a series of theologians and envoys: Sylvester Mazzolini drafted a heresy case, Cardinal Cajetan had instructions to arrest him if he did not recant, and Johann Eck branded him a new Jan Hus. Among reformers, Huldrych Zwingli and others disputed his insistence on the real presence of Christ's body and blood in the Eucharist at the Marburg Colloquy of 1529, the one point of fifteen left unagreed.

When the peasants' revolts of 1524 turned into war, many peasants believed he would support them. He sympathised with some of their grievances but, in Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants, called on the nobles to "smite, slay, and stab" the rebels. In 1526 he wrote: "I, Martin Luther, have during the rebellion slain all the peasants". In 1539–1540 he advised Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse, to marry a second wife secretly and then to "tell a good, strong lie"; his biographer Martin Brecht calls it "one of the worst mistakes Luther made".

In 1523 he had advised kindness towards the Jews, aiming at their conversion. In 1543, in On the Jews and Their Lies and a second treatise, he called them "the devil's people" and advocated setting synagogues on fire, forbidding rabbis to preach, seizing property and expelling Jews "for all time". Josel of Rosheim blamed the plight of Saxony's Jews on him. According to the prevailing opinion among historians, this rhetoric contributed significantly to antisemitism in Germany; Johannes Wallmann argues that there was no continuity between Luther's thought and Nazi ideology.
sections.last:
Outlawed, Luther could not attend the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 and stayed at the fortress Veste Coburg from 24 April to 4 October, influencing from there Philipp Melanchthon's negotiations and the Augsburg Confession presented to Charles V on 25 June.

He had long suffered from ill health, including Ménière's disease, vertigo, fainting, tinnitus and a cataract in one eye, and from 1531 it deteriorated further: kidney and bladder stones, arthritis and a ruptured ear drum from 1536, and the effects of angina from December 1544. Poor health made him short-tempered and harsher in his writings. His last sermon, delivered at Eisleben on 15 February 1546, was according to Léon Poliakov "entirely devoted to the obdurate Jews", whom he wanted expelled from German territory.

He had travelled to help settle a dispute with the counts of Mansfeld that threatened his siblings' families in the copper mining trade, twice in late 1545 and again in early 1546. The negotiations were concluded on 17 February 1546. That evening he had chest pains; asked by his companions Justus Jonas and Michael Coelius whether he was ready to die trusting in Christ and confessing the doctrine he had taught, he answered a distinct "Yes". An apoplectic stroke deprived him of speech, and he died at 2:45 a.m. on 18 February 1546, aged 62, in Eisleben, the city of his birth. He was buried in front of the pulpit of the Schlosskirche in Wittenberg; Johannes Bugenhagen and Melanchthon held the funeral. His excommunication was still in effect.
sections.legacy:
Luther's theological beliefs form the basis of Lutheranism, though he himself insisted on "Christian" or "Evangelical" as the only acceptable names. He was the most widely read author of his generation: between 1500 and 1530 his works represented one fifth of all materials printed in Germany. His Bible influenced other vernacular translations, such as the Tyndale Bible, a precursor of the King James Bible; the Small Catechism remains in use, and Johann Sebastian Bach based chorale cantatas on his hymns.

The partnership with the Saxon elector was, for Martin Brecht, "the beginning of a questionable and originally unintended development towards a church government under the temporal sovereign". The Catholic Church has never lifted the excommunication of 1521, although Lutherans and Catholics have since agreed on a "common understanding of justification by God's grace through faith in Christ".

His writings against the Jews were taken up in Nazi Germany: the city of Nuremberg presented a first edition of On the Jews and Their Lies to Julius Streicher in 1937, and in 1941 seven Protestant regional church confederations cited Luther in agreeing with the yellow badge. Scholars debate whether it is anachronistic to view his work as a precursor of racial antisemitism; Roland Bainton wrote that his position "was entirely religious and in no respect racial". Since the 1980s Lutheran denominations have repudiated these statements. Reformation Day, which commemorates the Ninety-five Theses, is a public holiday in nine German states.

summary: Martin Luther (1483–1546), an Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, challenged the sale of indulgences in 1517, was excommunicated and outlawed in 1521, and gave the Reformation its German Bible, catechisms and hymns. He also wrote against the rebel peasants of 1525 and, in 1543, against the Jews.
references: Roland Bainton, Here I Stand: A Life of Martin Luther (Abingdon Press, 1950)
Scott H. Hendrix, Martin Luther: Visionary Reformer (Yale University Press, 2015)
Heiko Oberman, Luther: Man Between God and the Devil (Yale University Press, 2006)
notes: The article's lead says Luther 'authored' the Theses in 1517 and was excommunicated 'in January 1521'; the body gives 31 October 1517 and 3 January 1521. Body dates used.
Posting of the Theses: the article gives Melanchthon's statement, Iserloh's objection and Treu's 2006 find of Rörer's note; the section gives the first two only, for space.

The 1525 event joins the tract against the peasants and the marriage (both 1525) to stay within eight events. The quotation 'I, Martin Luther, have during the rebellion slain all the peasants' is dated 1526 by the article.

Death: the article says the 'final journey' was 'to Mansfeld', that he went 'to Mansfeld twice in late 1545' with a third visit in early 1546, and that he died 'in Eisleben'. It does not say where the negotiations sat. The section therefore speaks of a dispute 'with the counts of Mansfeld' and does not name the place of negotiation.

The joint understanding on justification: the article's sentence gives '1999 and 2006, respectively' for three parties (Lutheran World Federation, Methodists, the Catholic Pontifical Council), so the years cannot be matched with certainty; the section gives no year.
'Nine German states' is a count of the article's list (Brandenburg, Bremen, Lower Saxony, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg).

The summary's last sentence ('remain the most disputed parts of his record') is a drafting judgement, not a statement in the article; the editor may prefer to cut it. The article does say the Philip of Hesse affair 'caused lasting damage to Luther's reputation' and reports the scholarly debate on the anti-Jewish writings.
The second 1543 treatise is 'Vom Schem Hamphoras und vom Geschlecht Christi' (On the Holy Name and the Lineage of Christ).
The article spells Melanchthon's first name both Philip and Philipp; both occur in the sections as the article has them near each passage. The editor may wish to settle on one.

Left out for space: the hymn catalogue, the soul-sleep discussion, his writings on Islam and the Turks, the Zwickau prophets and Karlstadt's reforms in detail, the children's names and dates, the swan legend, the Nazi-era material beyond Streicher and the 1941 statement (Sasse, Himmler, Probst, Goldhagen), Tovia Singer's judgement, and Mark U. Edwards's suggestion that the late polemics were partly the product of his state of health.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js, or its Further reading list), chosen by the editor.
